utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. President and Your Honours. The next witness is ready. He is, as the Court knows, a videolink witness. He is present in his remote location. I just wanted to make sure that I'm getting an English translation. I'm not hearing anything in my headphones, or I wasn't a few minutes or few seconds before. It's working, okay. Mr. President, this next witness has requested that he be granted two protective measures, that is, pseudonym and facial distortion. And I believe this witness would be Witness UU and has requested those protective measures. I could also proceed to inform the Trial Chamber of the relevant portions of the indictment that this testimony will relate to. First of all, paragraph 7 and paragraph 11 of the background part of the indictment regarding coordination with the army of Croatia, the HV, as well as systematic pattern of discrimination against the Bosnian Muslim population; paragraphs 14 through 17, which relate to the superior authority of both of the accused; the general allegations contained in paragraphs 18 through 21, which relate to international armed conflict and widespread and systematic campaign; paragraphs 27 through 30, 33, and 34 of count 1, which relate to the detention facilities, presence of the accused in the detention facilities, beatings of detainees; paragraphs 37 and 39, which are part of counts 2 through 5, regarding presence of the accused in the Heliodrom and the use of detainees on front-line positions for forced labour; and finally paragraphs 45, 49, and 50, which are part of counts 9 through 12, relating to torture and beatings of detainees. Mr. President, we have here in the courtroom a sheet of paper on which we have written the name and the pseudonym of the witness, and as well as his birth date, and I believe that Mr. Dubuisson also has such a piece of paper in his possession, and I would ask that he show that piece of paper to the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, before we move on to this stage, I wish to say that we shall object to these measures. So before you rule on the application, please allow me to state our reasons, and I would like to do it in private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is some background noise, some interference. I wonder if that can be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you are now being a shown a piece of paper. I simply ask if you can tell us whether on that piece of paper you find your correct name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the sheet of paper is my name, and my date of birth is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as you've heard, the Trial Chamber has granted the request for protective measures, so you are going to be given the pseudonym "UU." And I will ask that during your testimony, please don't disclose to us or say your name or give us any other information which might result in your being identified publicly. Now, Witness, let me ask you, are you a Bosnian Muslim who lived in the area of Travnik and Turbe in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before 1993, did you actually live in Germany for a number of years during the 1980s and early 1990s and work in Germany during those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes, I worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you return to the Travnik area in Central Bosnia in November of 1991, from Germany to try to start your own company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in 1991 and 1992, were you living in that area, Travnik and Turbe, with your wife and with your nine-year-old son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, on this line of questions, in July of 1992, were you mobilised into the civilian police in the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this after the conflict had started in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the Serbs were attacking Muslims and Croats in various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- at various times during the direct, I'm going to refer to one or two maps. Exhibit number 1 is the big map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's the only map in evidence which contains all the locations that the witness is going to talk about today, and -- although later in the examination, the Trial Chamber will find that most of the places during the direct will be found in Exhibit number 2. But perhaps just if we could -- and it's not as easy to do it through the video-conference link, but I wanted to indicate with the witness and the Trial Chamber the location of Travnik, which is not in the area that the Trial Chamber has heard a great deal about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, if Exhibit number 1 is there with you - it's the map which Mr. Dubuisson has - I wonder if you take a pencil, place a circle around the place called Travnik that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber's information - maybe I could just speed it along - if you look at the vertical axis on this map and the number "3" on the vertical axis, and then if you move across horizontally to the "E" on the top, Travnik is located just west of Zenica in Central Bosnia, in the area north and west of Sarajevo, at the intersection roughly of the "3" and the "E" on the vertical and horizontal axes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you marked Travnik and Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe -- Mr. President, in the map the word appears -- big word appearing "Bosnia," for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Travnik's located just under the "S" in "Bosnia." Maybe that would -- okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just asked you about July of 1992, when you were mobilised into the civilian police. Can you tell us, at about that time and in the months that followed, did you attempt to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions I tried to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I had no problems with going back to the Federal Republic of Germany and considering that many, many years before the outbreak of hostilities I had left to work there. However, when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina started, it was impossible for me to immediately -- that is, in the first several months, it was impossible for me to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in March of 1993, were you able to get permission then to leave and to go up to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received permission in March 1993, and with this permission, I received a legal travel document from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, because without a travel document, I could not travel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this trip, then, to Germany in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first and primary reason for my departure was the fear for myself and my own family, because I was facing the war for the first time and the shooting and all that. And to be perfectly honest, I wanted to prepare the ground to pull out my wife and my family also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you travel to Germany on the 31st of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your wife and your son remain behind in Travnik at that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. However, they did stay in the area of Travnik; that is, they were about 20 kilometres from the Travnik town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you remain in Germany for approximately two months, until the end of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then did you go to Split in Croatia on your way back home from Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I travelled between Zagreb, Split. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again going back Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, I will ask you to go back to Exhibit number 1, and if you could place a circle around the place called Split.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can then put that on the ELMO and ... Witness, is Split a city that's located on the Adriatic coast in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, tell us what happened when you arrived in Split?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to request -- because you don't have the statement that we received, and perhaps we shouldn't just keep giving the same explanation. I kind of assume what the witness will say, but I see no relevance. I see no connection. Perhaps my colleague is leading the witness. What is the connection, Split and these things, with these two accused? So owing to the time that we have - and we have been warned several times - perhaps the Prosecutor can be advised to just skip over everything that is not relevant and to focus on what could conceivably concern these two accused. Otherwise, we are faced with a very long and winding road from -- through the rugged terrain of Bosnia and Croatia, and it has nothing to do with our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that is a very constructive suggestion. Mr. Stringer, could you lead this witness as soon as possible so that we could arrive at the essential point of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I intend to do that. And with perhaps a little bit of cooperation from my learned colleagues, and perhaps the approval of the Trial Chamber, I could pose questions in a way that would advance us more quickly. However, I must say - and really, I couldn't put it better than Mr. Krsnik just put it - this witness encountered a very long and winding road throughout Croatia and Bosnia, and it is a story which, in part, does not relate directly to these two accused, but it relates very directly, and in our view is very relevant, to other important parts of the case such as the existence of a campaign, widespread and systematic campaign, directed against Bosnian Muslims throughout the region, as well as the involvement of the Republic of Croatia and Croatian authorities. And so that is relevant. It is, as I mentioned, expressly alleged in the paragraphs of the indictment which I cited at the beginning of this afternoon's proceedings, and so there is an interesting story which is relevant and which, in our view, must be told; however, I agree that it is one that perhaps we might be able to move through a little more quickly before we arrive to those parts of the testimony which relate most directly to the accused themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, let me just ask you, then, did you arrive in Split on the 31st of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also there, then, on the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you at the bus station with other Bosnian Muslims who were trying to then get back into Bosnia from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, please -- although I know this is a painful story for you, could you tell us briefly what happened to you and other Bosnian Muslims who were at the bus station in Split on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was waiting to get a ride to Bosnia by any means, along with the others, either by bus or by getting a lift from either a humanitarian convoy or UNHCR, I saw a large number of civilian policemen of the Republic of Croatia who were checking documents, the documents of civilians at the bus station and across from the bus station in the Emona transit station. I felt no fear or trepidation, because I was a civilian and I had proper travel documents on me with a German visa stamped in it and so on. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Let me ask you a couple of questions, then, about that. Were you approached by some members of the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was approached by members of the Croatian police, and they asked me for my documents. And as I said, I gave it to them without any fear or any anxiety because I knew that I was clean. I gave them my travel document. They looked at it. They read out my name, and they said, "You are a balija" --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- "Come with us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the police station in Split, which was right at the -- across from the station and across the railroad tracks and near the ferry station Emona. There is a police station right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us briefly what transpired -- let me first ask you first: Were there other Bosnian Muslims at the police station when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many in the yard. There were women, men, children. And there were a lot of them in the building itself, and I cannot give you an exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you when you were taken inside the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not want to tire you too much. We heard that this was Split and that this was the Republic of Croatia, and we heard what the treatment was of this body of the Republic of Croatia towards this witness. Again, my question is: What does this have to do with the indictment and with my client? I have to ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, you promised us that you could get over this part of the story as soon as possible so that we could get to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm doing my best, Mr. President. The Heliodrom is at the end. I have been given two witnesses to lead this evidence, and if I have to use every minute of it, over two hours - I'm sorry - to lead this evidence, and I'll use every minute of it, over the objections of counsel if I have to, and I'm going to try to move quickly. But if -- I'm concerned about objections placing me in a position where we're not at the Heliodrom by the end of the time that I have been given. If the counsel's willing to allow me to lead this witness, to put to him leading questions in order to move us more quickly along, then I will do it, but I assert that all of this is all relevant to allegations which are in the indictment, not all of which relate directly to his client. But if we engage in a lengthy debate here while the clock is ticking, then it's going to prevent the Prosecution from leading the evidence. It's an attempt, perhaps, to do just that, but it's all relevant. And unless the Trial Chamber expressly rules that it's not relevant and that it doesn't want to hear this evidence -- this witness's evidence, then I will skip portions of his story. But I would like to lead all of this, all of which is relevant and which will result, at the end, in direct testimony about the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will no longer object. And whatever he -- the witness is going to stay in terms of evidence, until he comes to the Heliodrom, will have nothing to do with this case and with our client, and that is basically all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what if I say that before you come to the Heliodrom that leading questions are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We really hope you could get over this part as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. President. Certain aspects of this witness's testimony are a bit difficult to do in leading questions. If I could say, it's -- it's not a pleasant story, but I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to -- I'll continue to ask you questions. I'm sure that you've heard and that you understand the discussion that's taken place here in the courtroom. So let me ask you, when you arrived in the police station headquarters in Split, were you beaten by Croatian police? Was your passport taken away from you, ripped up, and was all the money that you had with you, some 16.000 German marks, also taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct that I was beaten, mistreated without any reason, as an animal, insulted me, took my money away, tore up my travel document and told me, "You used to have it. Now you don't have it. Isn't that clear?" And another policeman again hit me in the face, knocked me down, and I lost consciousness, and I was covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also take your personal property, your watch, your suitcases, your gold necklace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is all correct. They took everything away from me, a golden bracelet, a watch, personal effects, papers that I had, luggage, everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you then handcuffed and placed in a van along with approximately other -- 14 other Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was placed in handcuffs, and they loaded us on the van, like a police van, with the other civilians and locked us up in that van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these other civilians, were these other Bosnian Muslim men who were in Croatia for various reasons, who were also then residents or whose families were residents of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of their families lived in Bosnia, and many of their families also lived in Croatia. They worked in the concrete factory in Split or in other towns. They would come and visit them. They lived with them and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you were placed in this police van, were you and the others driven for about four or five years to the Croatia-Bosnia-Herzegovina border crossing at a place called Kamensko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They took us there without food or water, in a small confined space. And to us it seemed like an eternity. And finally they brought us to the Kamensko border crossing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the Kamensko border crossing, were you delivered by the Croatian police officers to approximately 20 HVO military police, soldiers, who were wearing white belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived then or when you were delivered to the HVO military police, were you and the others then beaten for a couple of hours at that location by the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. And moreover, we were beaten by civilians who were ethnic Croats. And the policemen who allowed them to do that, this was done by the civilians who simply found themselves at this border crossing at Kamensko at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, did these HVO military police, did they place you and the others in a van and take you to the town called Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is Tomislavgrad also known as Duvno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the real name of Tomislavgrad. This is the one that I'm -- have been familiar with for many years. However, later on this town was given a new name, which is Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, on Exhibit Number 1, the town is called Tomislavgrad. On Exhibit Number 2, it's called Duvno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you would take Exhibit Number 1, place a circle around "Tomislavgrad." And while you're doing that, I'll ask you the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you arrived at Tomislavgrad, were you and the other prisoners placed in an old building that was a former convent, and were there already about 50 or 60 other prisoners there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you guarded by HVO military police wearing white belts during the time that you were at Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were guarded by members of the HVO, of the police, that is, while we were detained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you and other prisoners, then, placed into a large room which was divided into cages with metal, metal that's used for construction purposes, into an improvised jail in this old building in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you arrived at this location in Tomislavgrad, were you and the others beaten by the military police who used iron bars and other forms of instruments to beat you and the others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for your benefit, what he circled on the map is not the town that we were referring to, the thing that we see on the map, just so that you have full information. In other words, what witness has circled as the town that he was asked to circle by the Prosecutor is not the town that was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's have a look at that map again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. If the map could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now we're seeing that you circled a place called Livno. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot find Tomislavgrad, but it is close to Livno.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Livno --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if it exists on this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the town of Tomislavgrad or the municipality of Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the town of Tomislavgrad. And from what I knew, that was an abandoned monastery or something like that. It was an old building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you -- during the time that you spent at this location in Tomislavgrad, were you placed in locations where other dead persons were being kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, I was carried to the attic of this building where I saw a number of dead bodies of civilians. And on another occasion when I was mistreated and beaten, without even asking me any questions, they just cursed me and hurled insults at my family and the political structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They took me outside under a large tree, and under this tree, I saw several dead bodies of civilians lying around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you just tell us briefly how often you were beaten there and what was your condition finally when you were taken away from Tomislavgrad some 22 days later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me when I say that they came and beat me -- they beat others, too. And they beat me every hour on the hour. And the ill-treatment and battery and provocation could last 30, 40, 45 minutes, up to one hour. I was bleeding; I was looking at the puddles of my blood. And five, six, seven of them jumping off the table on me, ill-treat me, beat me with rifle butts, with fists, with boots, with iron rods, with batons. And I even begged them, "I beg you as friends, kill me. I just can't bear it any more."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mention that you were carried up to an attic. Is that because you were not able to walk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I could not walk. I was all broken up. I could not move. All the other prisoners were taken away somewhere - I don't know where - so that I was left alone, and they came and carried me away like a -- like a sack. I was all broken up. I was black and blue. And so they left me in this attic. And as they put me down, I just stayed there; that is, I couldn't turn either left or right. I was hungry. I was emaciated. I was tired. I was in pain. I was in blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were other dead bodies in that attic. How long were you left in that attic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, a question: What does it have to do with my client, and what does it have to do with the indictment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stringer, your question is too detailed, I believe. You might skip all those questions and details until the Heliodrom, which we are all interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, then were you kept in this place in Tomislavgrad for 22 days and then transferred to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you kept in a prison in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They kept us in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the prison in Ljubuski, did you find other prisoners there from places such as Mostar and Stolac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came across many prisoners; not only from Mostar and Stolac but also from surrounding places, towns such as Jablanica, Konjic, Bijele Polje, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your condition at Ljubuski was so bad that they expected you to die and that you were not taken out to perform labour like the others because of your condition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They would take me, but I could not stand up. I could not move. I was simply unable to make a single move, and I expected to die any moment. I thought I wouldn't be able to put up with that pain any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, now, after 12 days at the Ljubuski prison, were you and some others transferred to a place called Posusje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We were taken at night. We didn't know where we were going or why. When we got there, they said, "Posusje." I mean, I would have believed them even if they told me it was Milan, because I was -- yes, I knew all those areas before of Herzegovina, but I was semiconscious. I was barely aware of what was going on around me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll just simply refer the Trial Chamber to Exhibit 2, which has Posusje on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you remain at the Posusje detention facility for about nine days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you and others beaten frequently, both day and night, when you were at Posusje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us often both by day and by night, but I have to say much, much less than in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- the guards also at Posusje, were they members of the HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They all wore uniforms and white belts. So that was the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after nine days at Posusje, were you and some others then taken to a different place in the town of Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in Grude for about 18 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, were you kept in the cellar of an old house on the outskirts of the town of Grude?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you know why you were being moved around so frequently among these different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I could not really understand why they were moving us around, so I cannot say with any certainty. But from what I knew then and from what I know now, they were hiding us from the International Red Cross from Geneva, to avoid our registration, because if we were registered by the Red Cross, then -- well, one knows that then prisoners have their rights, that they may not be ill-treated or killed, they must be given food, and so on and so forth. At least that is what I think. I'm not sure about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this place in Grude, were the guards regular HVO soldiers, not military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after approximately 18 days at this house in Grude, then were you taken to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. They took us in a bus to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, by my count, that would be approximately the very beginning of August 1993. Does that sound right to you, the date of your arrival in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you -- as best as you recall, can you tell us what occurred when you arrived at the Heliodrom? What time of day was it and what occurred when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around noon. It was daylight. Everybody got off the bus except me because I could not move. So they took me, carried me, dragged me, whatever you care to call it. There were a number of soldiers, a number of HVO, lots of military policemen of the HVO with white belts, and one spoke to us and told us what this was the central prison of Herceg-Bosna, that its name was Heliodrom. And among other people there, I saw Juka Prazina, with his escort. He was wearing black. And they took me, asked me -- they asked, "What's the matter with him?" I dared not say that I had been all beaten and battered in the previous death camps, so that all I said was that I had been involved in a traffic accident. Of course, they knew what was wrong with me. It was just like that. So they took me to a cellar, and then Juka said very loudly and clearly, "No problem. We've got coffin for him. Quite broad. You know, the one from Sarajevo." That's what he said. And in that cellar, I spent a couple of hours leaning against a coffin in the cellar. It was very dark, and it was terrible stench. I don't know how large was the cellar or something. And some people were passing by. And I would every now and then pass out and then recover. And one of the soldiers who were passing by there, he saw me, he kicked me, and I cried out in pain. And then he said, "Look, this one is alive, so take him out of there." And they took me to the second floor of that building, and that was the so-called central prison of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you, were there any other coffins in this cellar that you've described, other than the one that you were standing by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say there were many of them. There could have been 10 or 12. I didn't count them. I didn't look around. As I said, they carried me. They just threw me there. And since it was the cellar, it was very murky. And I didn't try even to look or to count, and I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were taken upstairs to the second floor of that building, can you tell us what sort of room you were placed in, how many prisoners were in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a big metal door -- door with metal bars on the second floor with large locks. And you opened that door, and there was a passage behind it, and there were three rooms there. I was in the first one to the left. And there I found about 70, maybe 80, detainees. I was put -- thrown into a corner. There were no beds or chairs or tables or anything. We were all there. And I was in the corner of that room, of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the registrar Mr. Dubuisson show the witness what has been marked as Exhibit 20.10. It's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the registrar is going to show you a photograph, and I'm is going to ask you if you can identify any of the buildings that are shown in that photograph. If you see a building where you were kept, place a circle around it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could I ask the registrar to put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we're looking at the building that you've circled. Is that what you've described as the Central Military Prison and the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at least that is what they told us - I mean, members of the Croat Defence Council and members of the military police of the Croat Defence Council - when we arrived. Now, whether they meant this building, that that building was the central prison, or whether the Heliodrom as such was the central prison, I really can't say. But that is what they said, that this was the central prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this -- in any event, whatever its name is, is this the building where you were held after you arrived at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the building in which I kept throughout the time I was at the Heliodrom, and I never left that room or that building, nor did I go anywhere. I was non-stop -- I could not move because I was beaten just too badly, so that I spent there a certain period of time. That is, all the time that I was at the Heliodrom, all I could see were those four walls in that room on the second floor in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know approximately how many other prisoners were held in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that in that room, there were between 70 and 80 prisoners. I was one of them. In the next room, there were just as many, around 70 detainees. Indeed, the third one, there were again around 70 people. That is at least what people talked about, the detainees who could go out to go to the toilet, to the bathroom. And from that room, one could enter those other two. But they could not get out of this passage. They could not get past that huge locked door, metal door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did the other prisoners remain in that room all day with you when you were at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Other prisoners were taken at daybreak every morning to work, to dig trenches, to carry things, to build some fortifications. They were driven out every morning and came back in the evening. And as I could not move and I was waiting to die, I thought I would succumb to my open wounds, because I was non-stop in that one room. I could not move, and I was non-stop in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what are some of the locations where the other prisoners worked when they were taken out of your room? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know 100 percent when they came back in the evening tired, hungry, and thirsty, and so on and so forth, some of them would say they had worked in an area called Balinovac. Others said they worked on Santiceva. I don't know what that is or where that is. Others said again they were working near the department store. Others again, that they were on Bulevar. That is what I remember them saying when they would come back in the evening to that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who the prisoners were working for when they were working outside the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. Any answer would be speculation, because we just learned that he never once went out of the camp. So I do not think that any other kind of answer can be expected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we understand that it will be hearsay evidence, and we'll evaluate this evidence at a later stage. We understand this witness was in the cell all the day. So you may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you this: Did you ever see anyone come to the Heliodrom, into your building, into your cell to take prisoners out to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every morning, uniformed individuals came. They had white belts of the Croat Defence Council, whether they were military police or just soldiers, and they took them away to work every morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And based on what you saw and what you heard, do you know which units or which persons those prisoners were being taken to work for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't really know. He just knows what he was told. I was wondering, without offending the witness and hurting him - he's living through a lot of pain - could we move him on to evidence that affects the two accused? I think he's clearly suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President -- I'm sorry, Judge Clark. We are at that point right now, and I will try to bring it to greater focus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned military police came to take prisoners away. Did you see any other HVO personnel in your area, in your building where you were being held in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, I did see soldiers. I saw many with or without white belts, those who dropped in in that room either in the morning or in daytime or in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any commanders come or higher-level HVO personnel come into your area in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my own eyes, I saw on only two occasions Mr. Mladen Naletilic in that room. He was called Tuta. I repeat, it was only on two occasions that I saw him. And several times with soldiers and with those military HVO policemen, I saw Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela. Also in that room I saw Juka Prazina - they wouldn't stay long - and I saw other soldiers, military policemen, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you, if you can, to describe for us as best you recall each of the times that you saw Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, in your part of the Heliodrom. Can you describe for us on each of those occasions who he was with and what occurred when he was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, it was daytime. And as I say, I was alone in the room. And very many of them came; I mean soldiers, uniformed individuals, non-uniformed as well, a few of them. And they were practically at the entrance into that room, next to the door where you go into it. And they were talking amongst themselves. I could not hear what they were talking about or what was the subject they were talking about. And one of that group walked towards me, that is, moving towards a completely different part of the room, towards the corner of that room, and that one had an HVO uniform, and yelled at me and ordered me to stand up. "Don't you see who has come here to this room?" And I said, "I am sorry, sir. Please receive my apologies, but I cannot move. I cannot stand up. I am not well," and so on and so forth. And then he really started bellowing at me, that soldier or military policeman, and trying to make me stand up. And I, like a dog, tried to support me with the two hands, and I tried to hoist myself, but as I was about to stand up, he hit me with his fist in the stomach, and I bled at the mouth again, and I fell down again. And all those others were standing in the corner and talking about something. And that one presumably - I say one; only one who came and ill-treated me and beat me - perhaps he wanted to show off front of the others, to prove his valour, to prove what a tough guy he was, how he can beat a man who cannot -- who is unable to move. So I stayed there on the floor, and he moved away from me, and he asked me once again why was I there. Oh, come on. Why am I there? "Well, you locked me up." What does mean, "Why am there?" And they left that room. They could have been there -- I mean all of them there, 10, 15 minutes. I cannot say exactly, but they didn't stay long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the names of any of the others persons who were with Mladen Naletilic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that Mr. Armin Pohara, Mr. Rusmir Agacevic, and others, other soldiers, uniformed individuals, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said that soldier struck you in the chest, was Mladen Naletilic in a position to have seen that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a position to see that, and I am quite sure that he did see it, although he was at the other end of the room. And he was surrounded -- there were several of them in a group. But he could see the second -- the other end of the room where this one hit me and ill-treated me. But there were many of them, as I said. They were standing and talking. I don't know really what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned that you saw Mladen Naletilic on two occasions in the Heliodrom. You've just described one occasion. Let me ask you first: Have you just described for us the first time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first time, when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how long after your arrival in the Heliodrom this first encounter with Tuta took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could be perhaps 15, 20 days later. I can't really say exactly, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that it may be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll break for 90 minutes. We'll resume at 8.00 this evening. We have been advised if we have two accused, when we break for supper, that should be 90 minutes. We'll resume at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're still having some difficulties with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- the devices over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please try again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you described for us an encounter that you had with Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also before the break, you said that in fact you had two encounters or there were two times when you saw Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, in the Heliodrom. So my question to you now is: Could you please describe for us the second encounter that you had with Tuta in the Heliodrom, who was present, as best as you recall, and what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time when I saw Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, at the Heliodrom, again in the same room where I continued to stay, this was in the evening, it was night-time, and a lot of soldiers -- a lot of HVO soldiers entered and the military policemen with white belts. I cannot say the exact number. It could have been approximately 15. And Juka Prazina was among them. On that occasion, I saw Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela. They were at the door to that room. They were talking among themselves. They were saying something. I did not hear at all what they were saying because I was on the other end of the room. At one point, someone in the entourage of one of the soldiers, one of the men who were wearing HVO uniforms, a soldier near the door, hit a young man, a civilian, who was nearby. Another one approached him, and then they were shouting at him something. They were cursing him. They were mentioning Prozor. He was either from Prozor or near Prozor. And Juka Prazina was there with his dog, a German shepherd, and there was a great commotion there. I saw that this young man was bleeding. He was moaning. He was crying. At one point, Juka Prazina let his German shepherd dog loose. He turned him loose, and the dog assailed the young man, but he was pulled out of the room, and I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did this event take place in the room which you've described in which you were held during the time that you spent at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, because I want to mention I was -- throughout this time, I was in one and the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, can you tell us, please, the positions of Tuta and Stela, that is, Martinovic and Naletilic? Where were they located? What was their position when this incident occurred with the one prisoner from Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in a group, all of them together. And Mr. Naletilic did not beat the young man, nor did Mr. Martinovic beat or touch that young man, but they were in that same group of 13 to 15 soldiers. You see what I mean? There was a lot of people there, and as I mentioned, there were about 70 prisoners in the room. Everybody was there in a group near the door just as you entered the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe whether either Mr. Naletilic or Mr. Martinovic took any steps to stop the mistreatment of that young man from Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that they had done anything to either -- to stop. Maybe they were talking about it among themselves. Maybe they said, "Don't do it any more." I was at least 12 to 15 metres away. I was at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the very corner of it. It was a long room. But as I said, I did not see that anyone took any steps to defend the man, neither the two of them nor anyone else. Two maybe up to three soldiers attacked this young man. I don't know what they were doing and why they were talking among themselves. So I cannot say what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during those two times when you saw Mr. Naletilic in the Heliodrom, can you describe for us, please, his appearance, how he looked, how he was dressed on those occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform, and I want to point out that I was in a prone position, so I was looking from that vantage point. He was not a very tall man. He had eyeglasses, beard. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the colour of his hair, the colour of his beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was kind of greyish, greying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that -- first, let me ask you this: Do you know or did you learn during the time you were at the Heliodrom who the commander of the Heliodrom facility was? Who was in charge of that place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, personally I do not know who was the commander in the Heliodrom camp, nor did I hear about who the commander was. The only thing I can say is this: That the other prisoners who were from Herzegovina, Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, and so on, that they were saying as concerns certain soldiers and certain HVO men in uniform and the military police, when they entered countless of times to the rooms, day or night, those who were in the room with me were saying, "Well, these are the Tuta's men," and occasionally they would say, "These are the Stela's men," that is, that ones belonged to Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and the others to Vinko Martinovic, Stela. However, I repeat - and I stand by it - I personally do not know. But this is what the men from Herzegovina were saying. They were whispering about it. They were saying, "These belong to this one, and those belong to that one." I personally do not know. I did not see, nor do I know who the commander of the Heliodrom camp was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, also before the break you testified, I believe, that you saw Vinko Martinovic present in the Heliodrom on other occasions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him several --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead and complete your answer if I interrupted you. How many times did you see him in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him several times at the Heliodrom; that means in the room where I was staying. On all those occasions, he would come in just briefly with his escorts, entourage. I don't know how to describe it. And he would stay there very briefly in the room where I was staying. I don't know what they were saying, what they were talking about, as they had just came in, and then they would go out. On one occasion when I was alone in the room during the day - and as I said, I was gravely ill - a prisoner came, a prisoner who apparently had been at the Heliodrom for six or seven months. That means a lot longer than I was. And I heard that he was fixing the cars or something like that for these soldiers. He was tall and well built. He saw me bleeding from my mouth and my nose. Then he took me by my arms and by force took me to another room and asked that the door be unlocked. And he took me to some kind of an improvised infirmary in the hope that a physician would help me. There was a physician there in a white coat. He was dark-haired man. When I entered that room with him, I saw four or five soldiers with white belts and camouflage uniforms. They said, what were we doing there? What were we requesting? We asked the doctor. And the doctor said that I was ill and that I needed help. And one of the soldiers in white belt cursed my mother, even though he saw me for the first time in his life at that time. And he said, "Well, you came here to get medical treatment in Herceg-Bosna," and he hit me and kicked me in the stomach and head. And there was another one also in camouflage uniform, and he also jumped on me and beat me and knocked me down. I don't know their names. I simply do not know what they are. And there, I saw Vinko Martinovic, Stela, sitting there with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago you described one encounter which you had with Mladen Naletilic and others, including Vinko Martinovic, that he was present. I wanted to ask you now about other times when you saw Vinko Martinovic in the Heliodrom. And particularly, if you could just give us a rough idea how many other times you saw him when you were a prisoner at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate, I believe I saw him about five or six times in total. I want to point out, on several occasions, he came with some soldiers in HVO uniform, in the room. They were, again, talking something, but I don't know what they were talking about. Perhaps they stayed five to ten minutes in the room, and then they would leave. A moment ago I said when this man almost forcibly dragged me by my arms and when he took me to this improvised infirmary in the hope that a physician would help me, on that occasion I saw Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela, with another four, five, or six soldiers in this small room, in this improvised infirmary. And they were talking there. When I entered this room with this prisoner who had brought me there in the hope that a physician would help me, because I was bleeding from my mouth and my nose, one of the uniform soldiers with white belts jumped up and said -- cursed my mother. He insulted me and he said, "You came here to Herceg-Bosna to seek medical treatment." He punched me and kicked me in the face and stomach. And other soldiers jumped over, and they knocked me down on the floor. Mr. Vinko Martinovic saw this, but he himself did not hit me, nor did he approach me. I stayed in that room for perhaps 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- my next question, then, was: How did you know that this person you're calling Vinko Martinovic, Stela, how do you know that in fact that was who this person was? How did you know it was Stela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he -- when he had come to the room on previous occasions, previous days, the men from Herzegovina who were my fellow prisoners in the room said, "That is Stela. That is Martinovic." Someone said, "This is Vinko Martinovic." Another one would say, "This is Stela." So on several occasions when he was coming to the room, those men who were there with me in the room, these were men from Herzegovina who apparently knew him quite well, and they told me. I myself had never seen this man, Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela, before that. I had never heard of him, nor had I had any close encounters or dealings with before that, so I'm saying what the other prisoners who were there in this one and the same room were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there times when soldiers would come -- that other soldiers would come - not Stela personally, but that other soldiers would come - to take prisoners for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many soldiers in camouflage uniform and white belts who came regularly every morning and were taking prisoners to forced labour. I want to point out that they would come every day, and in the evening these men would come back. However, also in the evenings, the man in uniform again would come and would be taking prisoners at night, 9.00, 10.00, 11.00, even midnight, even one after midnight, would take two or three, sometimes one of them. Why they were taking them, where they were taking them, that I don't know. I had no knowledge of that, but I know 100 per cent when, at the break of dawn, four, five, or six would come. "Come on. Get out," they would say quickly, and they would just come out. And as I said, I always stayed alone in that room, behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how long did you then remain a prisoner at the Heliodrom complex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed exactly 45 days, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just briefly describe then where you were taken when you left the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One night late at night, they were taking out prisoners from the room and apparently from other rooms. There were a lot of soldiers at that time. It was the largest number of soldiers and uniformed policemen that I saw that night. I was taken, carried. I could not straighten up. I was bent over almost to the ground, and the other prisoners told the soldiers that they needed to help me down some staircase to -- not the main entrance to the building where we had been -- where we had entered when we were first brought into the Heliodrom but another entrance. We saw a lot of small buses like mini-buses and vans, and we were all made to board those mini-buses. And then they drove us a long time, through the night. And at one point, these buses stopped, and we were transferred to large buses, coaches. We were told that those large buses could not negotiate the switchbacks that apparently we had been going on previously, so they used those small buses to get there. We were eventually brought to the mechanical engineering school, and there were some sports fields behind it, and that's where we were brought. And there were a lot of women and children and a lot of civilians there, and there was a lot of screaming and yelling. So we were brought there in this plateau in front of the mechanical engineering school. Again, I heard that from somebody else. Had they told me that this was a soccer field, I would have accepted that, because I had never been to Mostar before, and I did not know these places, the school of mechanical engineering or any other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, at this location, the school of mechanical engineering, did you join about 300 other Muslims in that location, and then were you all put on buses at that location and moved out to a different place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Two hours later, in this sports field or the plateau at the school of mechanical engineering, we were placed on the buses. And I personally saw Mr. Juka Prazina there, who had come there, and he was telling everybody, "Don't worry. Everything's going to be all right. I will escort you." I heard him talk to the drivers, giving them some kind of instructions. But we were placed on these buses, and again they drove us for a long, long time without food or water. I could not sit in a passenger seat, but rather, I lay on the floor. And after - I can't say exactly - six, seven, eight hours, they brought us to the city of Sibenik, to the port there. We arrived at the port there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can inform the Trial Chamber, Sibenik is on the Adriatic coast of Croatia. It is not found on Exhibit 2. It is found on Exhibit 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me go back to asking you a series of questions for the remainder of your testimony in the same manner in which we were working through some of the earliest part of your testimony. When you and the others arrived at Sibenik in Croatia, were you met by Croatian police and also HVO military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We were met at the port in the Sibenik -- in the port of Sibenik. There were a lot of them. I can't give you a number but over 50 of them. There was a lot of civilians, too, the civilian population, men, women, who offered us food, some biscuits and juice. And we were allowed to take that; we were not forbidden by either the Croatian police or the HVO. Some people took some of these offerings. Some washed up. And I will never forget that these civilians in the city of Sibenik met us in a brotherly way, in a friendly way, and offered us these comforts in food and drinks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, then, were you and the others who travelled with you down from Mostar, were you put on a ferry and taken out to a place called Obonjan island?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. They put us all on a large ferry and took us to an island, which is called Obonjan. Again, I point out, this is what they said that it is called. I had never been before. This is what they were saying, Obonjan. Fine, it's Obonjan then. We were all brought there non-stop. The civilian police was there, and the HVO police were also there. We were all brought to this island, and there we found, in my estimate, about 1.000 civilians, men, women, children, the elderly, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, it's my understanding that you personally spent a little over one month on Obonjan island. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that time, you and the other persons who were there were sleeping in tents on this island?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. We slept in tents on the island.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some time after your arrival, then, representatives of the UNHCR, the High Commissioner for Refugees, and the International Red Cross arrived along with a representative from the Bosnian embassy in Zagreb, and they arranged for your transfer and the transfer of others from that location to Split, and then on to Istanbul in Turkey; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Everything you said is correct, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you arrived in Istanbul sometime during October 1993, and you remained in Turkey for approximately 10 to 12 months receiving medical treatment for the injuries that you had received; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The treatment was long and arduous. I took a lot of medications. I was bedridden for a long time. I received a lot of injection. Also, all my teeth had been knocked out. My ribs had been broken, the left shoulder, the right leg also. And like others, I received adequate treatment there and medical care and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, throughout this entire time of your being a prisoner in these many locations, did you have any contact with your wife and your son? Did they have any idea what had happened to you during all that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had no idea about it, nor did they know anything about my whereabouts or what was happening to me. Also, I assert that I, myself, did not know what was going on with my wife and my only son. And again, as I said, throughout this time, we had no access to the media, the television, radio, or newspapers, nor did I have any other avenue to find out what was going on with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, I understand that then you were reunited in Travnik with your family in August of 1994 and then you returned to -- you went to Italy in 1996, where you again underwent medical treatment for your injuries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not go back to Travnik exactly but to the area of Travnik. And for a while, I was there. However, as my physical condition and my mental condition worsened, because I had lost over 22 kilogrammes of my body weight in these death camps and my condition deteriorated, and in 1996, under auspices of a humanitarian organisation, I went for medical treatment in Italy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, my last question to you: During the entire time that you were in these various locations being held as a prisoner, did anyone ever inform you why you had been arrested or why you were being held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never informed why I had been arrested, why I had been kept in detention, and why had they so brutally destroyed my life. But I also wish to mention that during this ill-treatment, battery, and all the encounters and everything that happened during my stay in those camps, I can say honestly, because that is something that I could see, that all those soldiers, those military policemen, all those uniformed individuals of the HVO kept saying that my brothers or parents or friends or neighbours in Central Bosnia were beating and slaughtering and persecuting Croats in Central Bosnia. And I realised they were taking it out on us only because we were from Central Bosnia and some others who came from other parts of Bosnia. But whatever the case, those soldiers who beat me and maltreated me, who broke my body, they cursed my Muslim mother, Muslim children, the president, Alija Izetbegovic, the faith, the ethnicity, and that is what I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Before you start, I have to remind you that this witness is also a victim, so do put your question in a decent way and in a grace manner; otherwise, we'll stop you. You may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Somehow, I must say I always feel somewhat embarrassed when I am warned of things of which I do not think one needs to warn anyone. But now you prompt me to tell you which is my position in this cross-examination, and especially in view of the warning the other day by Judge Clark, so that I will say immediately that in this cross-examination, the Defence will check all of the allegations heard during the direct examination on the basis of the statements and some other documents which we were given today. And the Defence, they are to put it to the witness that he has not been to -- that he was not in a place that he says he was, and the Defence will try, because of the investigative work that we have done, that we have never found him on any list, unlike others. And I shall, therefore, try during this cross-examination to show this Chamber perhaps a different picture of this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my first question will be -- and this time, I will start - that may come as a surprise - from the end of the examination-in-chief. And I will ask you, Witness -- I'm sorry, I forgot to introduce myself. I am counsel for Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and I will ask you some questions. And I always do my best to make them as concise as possible in order to elicit the shortest answers and as complete as possible. So, Witness, will you please listen carefully to what I ask you, and bear in mind that we speak the same language, and therefore, make a break -- only after you have heard my question in full, only then start answering, in order to avoid speaking over one another, because in that case, the interpreters cannot do their job. Thank you for your cooperation. Witness UU, isn't -- wasn't the island of ^ Obonjan a refugee camp for all inhabitants, and in particular for Bosniaks who had fled when the war raged to that refugee camp where the Republic of Croatia provided the necessary care for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you expecting an answer from me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps for many people it may have been a refugee camp in which the Republic of Croatia offered all the necessary care, but that was not my case, because I and others were non-stop supervised by the police, uniformed and civilian police. And also, why didn't they let me, me and those others, to leave this rock? Because we had a way to go. Why were they kept under surveillance? And we were not allowed to move anywhere, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to go anywhere from that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many days did you spend in that refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that refugee camp, I spent about a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from that refugee camp or settlement, or whatever you care to call it, weren't you allowed to go anywhere you wanted from that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout that time, we were not allowed to go where we wanted, but later on, thanks to the UNHCR, and the pressure of the International Red Cross, the UNHCR, and other institutions, it was only then that we were allowed to leave, and that is when we were transferred to Turkey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the International Red Cross come there? I mean, when did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I saw representatives of the UNHCR, and other representatives of the International Red Cross, and a representative of the embassy - I mean, Bosnian - from Zagreb. They came there after I had been there for about a month, I say. They took pictures of us. They made sort of collective passports, collective travel documents, and took our particulars, and it was then that we left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, when exactly did you leave for Turkey, and how long exactly did you stay in Turkey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to -- I and others went to Turkey in November 1993, and I stayed in Turkey for about a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you returned in November 1994 to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To Bosnia I returned in August 1994. But I said that it was about a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is eight months, and there's quite a difference between eight months and a year. But it doesn't matter right now. You say that you spent 30 days on Obonjan. That is what you told us a moment ago. If you arrived there on the 1st of September and if you spent 45 days at the Heliodrom, then it was the 15th of September. That means that you spent more than two and a half months at Obonjan. I think these are significant differences. Do you remember those dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to remember the dates now, and it was difficult for me then. What I'm saying is I was there for about a month. I was very severely ill, and I did not have a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can we agree that you said today that you -- that you were at the Heliodrom for 45 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you got there on the 1st of August, then it was on the 15th of September that you set off to the refugee camp. And if you were a month at Obonjan, then it is the 15th of October. And you told us a moment ago that it was late November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I did not say it was late November. I said November. But it is also possible that we left in late October. So I'm very sorry. Really, I apologise for five or ten days. I didn't keep a diary; I wasn't allowed to, and I wouldn't have been able to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And tell me, when were you arrested in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, 1993, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all your statements it says the 31st of May. But it doesn't matter. Tell me, do you remember a letter which you wrote to the Minister of the Interior in 1996, that is, His Excellency, the Minister of the Interior -- of the Ministry of the Interior, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Avdo Habib? Do you remember writing him a letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe you have that letter that -- if not, then, my learned friend -- I do not have any more copies. Could Their Honours also be given the copies of that letter? There is also a translation into English. You were so kind enough to give them to us today. It was very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately the interpreters do not have copies of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have questions to ask about this letter, and I should like Their Honours to know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the letter that counsel is referring to, we did provide it to the Defence; however, I told or I informed Mr. Meek at the time that we were providing it out of an abundance of caution and that I had no intention of using it during the direct examination and that if they intended to use it themselves, they needed to make the necessary arrangements, so I have only two copies with me. I suppose we could make copies if it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We have three; one here and your two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to have one also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness has one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Again, just being careful, we faxed it to Mr. Dubuisson today, so he does have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please also have copies of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
