utterances.text: We better copy it and distribute it. Well, Mr. Krsnik, we believe it is not the first day for this trial. You must know that if you want to use any document, please make copies beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I received it -- and I am really grateful to my learned friend. I appreciate it. I appreciate his giving it to me. But I received it before the hearing started. I looked at it during the break, and I saw some very interesting things in it. There is a very important question here for the Defence. You will hear what it is about in no time at all. But since my learned friend has given it to us, then I thought that everybody had been supplied with this document. Perhaps this was a misunderstanding between me and my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We believe it is your responsibility to have those documents copied and furnished to everybody in this courtroom because you are using this document, not the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry, and I really apologise. But my question is: When? It was ten minutes before the hearing. And I went through it during the break, so I didn't have time to do that. And we have to remember that we started at 5.00; now it's 9.00 -- no, no, I'm not trying to defend myself. I'm not trying to defend myself. Now we have this whole story about a letter. All I wanted to do is read a sentence and the witness to answer me. If that is a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my only observation is we had quite a lengthy break in which ten copies could easily have been made. It is a document which counsel obviously decided he wanted to use. And his co-counsel was informed that we were simply providing it out of an abundance of caution, and that if they wanted to do anything with it, they would have to make the necessary copies or arrangements. I don't have anything more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, if that happens again, we will certainly bar you from using any documents which you did not prepare an extra copy for us, because it takes us a lot of time in this courtroom. And today, we have to sit very late, as you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I suggest, perhaps, there's another area that counsel could move on to, and then we could come back to this point when the copies are distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can you? You may ask other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be so kind and tell us if the Red Cross ever came to the Heliodrom, the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the International Red Cross visited the Heliodrom on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once or twice they came to the room in which I was. But all the prisoners crowded towards the door, towards them, so that they rushed to meet them. And as I was not able to move, I could not stand up, approach them, and try to push my way through those 70 or so prisoners in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And only because of that, you mean they simply could not see you; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they could see all 70 of us in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why didn't they register you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not register us because the military policemen with white belts pushed them out, and they were also -- they were also wearing uniforms, and they were pushing away the representatives of the International Red Cross. They would be there for 10, 15, maybe 20 minutes. So some next to them were maybe registered, but that is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that when the Red Cross came? Was it in daytime or in the evening or at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once they came in daytime. Once it was late afternoon, as far as I can remember. It was afternoon sometime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say daytime. Was it always like that, lots of people in your room? Didn't they go -- you told us today how they went to work daily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say 100 percent, that 100 percent of them went every day. I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that you were not registered because the Red Cross was forced out of your room? Are you saying that somebody dared push out the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite true, even worse. They were tearing up the documents of those who had been registered. Soldiers sometimes tore up even that. Now, if they could tear up such documents and drive them out, because had they been afraid of the Red Cross, they wouldn't have kept us under lock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, you said -- and I hope to repeat. Did you personally see those registration papers issued by the International Red Cross torn up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it, but other detainees said, "He got mine and tore it, and he was about to tear my arm off, too."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But today you said you didn't know who was the Heliodrom commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you said today when asked by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness and the counsel are speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask Mr. Dubuisson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, you give difficult times to the interpreter. Wait until we hear the answer from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning, you were doing very fine. We could follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask Mr. Dubuisson to give you the statement that you made to the investigators of this Tribunal. So will you please take it. Witness UU, will you please look at page 7, third passage, last sentence. You say -- in it, you stated to The Hague investigators the following: "During that period of time, Aleksovski was the commander of the Heliodrom." And you say, "Other detainees told me that Zlatko Aleksovski" - and now you are giving the full name, the first and the last name - "was not in command of the Heliodrom in the very beginning and that he came later." Then the next sentence: "We were visited by ICRC representatives in August 1993. Three of them came to our room to register us. They managed to register about 15 to 20 detainees, and then Zlatko Aleksovski, together with four or five military policemen, threw them out of the room." In your statement which you gave to the investigators and what you told us today is complete variance. Besides, here the name of the commander is mentioned three times, and his full name, and you point at him as the culprit for the Red Cross's failure to register you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I never met Mr. Aleksovski, nor did I see him; however, all that I said in my statement I continue to say under full responsibility that that is what I heard from other detainees. I am not sure about anything, nor did I have any knowledge, nor did I know who the commander was. It was thought that the detainees talked among themselves, now they say this, now they said that, and I didn't attach much attention to that. I say to this day that I do not know who that was, bearing in mind that I was in a very poor state and that I was fainting often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness UU, who was in the room when you were taken to the doctor? Was that the person whom you mentioned to the Prosecutor today when you told us about this time when you were taken to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was in the room. A detainee from another room came, and he got me by my trunk at my shoulders and practically drew me with him to the doctor in that makeshift infirmary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who else was there in that makeshift infirmary, apart from the doctor and yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four or five uniformed individuals. Some had military belts, white, and one of them was Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please be so kind now as to read the third passage. It begins on the same page. And see how you describe it to The Hague investigators. "The doctor told me to try to stand upright, straight, or to touch the floor with my hands. I told him that I was not able to do that. Then this soldier started beating me. Aleksovski did not say or do anything. The doctor was laughing all the time. I think that Aleksovski enjoyed the scene." So my first question is: What is the doctor's name, if you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly what the name of that physician was. However, I can say --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I can tell you that he was at the hospital in Bijeli Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not know then what the doctor's name was, nor do you know that today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have known, but it is possible I have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is what I am asking you, because two lines above that you give the name the doctor. This is: "He carried me to the doctor, whose name was Djeko."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what I heard him being called, but that could have been a nickname. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as Vinko Martinovic is concerned, there's no "V" or "M." There's no initials, let alone full name of him. Will you please read that whole page, if it's not too difficult. You'll see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not difficult for me to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll see that you never mentioned him. You never mentioned anyone except Aleksovski, and this is the fifth time that you mentioned him as a person who was there, who was in charge, and was very close to you -- in close proximity to you. How did he look at all, this Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. When I came to the infirmary to see the doctor, the person was well built, built up, big muscles, I think that it is the same person who had come to the room previously of whom the fellow prisoners who were there with me said that it was Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. But, sir, you never mentioned him during any of the events that you described here. No one except for Mr. Aleksovski, in fact, did you mention. That is on the 17th or 18th of September, 1997. Was your memory better in 1997, or is it better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, if in 1997 no one asked me or -- how shall I put it? If nobody inquired -- excuse me, but you have to realise that I was ill and that I could not -- that I cannot recall all the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, why did you not mention Mr. Aleksovski today regarding these events? That's number one. In fact, you never mentioned him, and you said that you did not know the name of the commander, and half of your statement is filled with "Mr. Aleksovski."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today nobody asked me about him, and I have to tell you, I was only answering the questions that were asked of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. When you were at the physician's, was Mr. Aleksovski there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. There were five or six soldiers. I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me now, is what you stated to the investigators not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it's not true, but my mental state at that time, I cannot recall all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we go to the private session for a minute, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and on which occasion was he at the Heliodrom and with whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him twice at the Heliodrom. He was with Juka Prazina, Armin Pohara, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and the other entourage and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Naletilic, Armin Pohara, Mr. Agacevic were together, and that is when you saw Mr. Tuta with them, what, for the first time, for the second time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the second time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Aleksovski also there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that. A number of faces passed in front of me. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you look at page 6 of your statement, please, the fourth paragraph, first sentence. Here you say that Aleksovski was there too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please. I could not see well, nor were they close to me. That is what the prisoners who were around me said. One of them may have said, "There's Aleksovski too." So I -- that means that I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, how did you know that that was Mr. Naletilic? Were you also told by others regarding him that it was him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The prisoners who were from Herzegovina, from Stolac, Capljina, Mostar, Konjic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you please describe Mr. Naletilic. How tall was he? What was his build?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed him from a prone position. He was wearing eyeglasses. He was not tall. He had greying hair, and then he had his hair parted to the side, and that's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his build? How much could he have weighed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not weigh him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, Witness, you did not, but was he well built? Was he built like you? Was he built like me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was not well built. I think -- I can say he was rather thin, than not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, this soldier who hit someone there at the end of the hallway, was that a military policeman? Is that what you said today? When they were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was either a military policeman or a soldier. They were together in the escort, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why they had come? What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know why they came. I don't know what they were talking about. I did not hear anything at all. I don't know why they had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please be so kind and tell me -- I'm going to show you a photograph now. I think it was the same that was shown to you by -- the same one you were given -- you were shown by my learned friend, that is, the Exhibit 20.10. And I will have a couple of questions regarding this photograph. Will you be so kind and tell me where your room was? If you can take a pointer and show it in this building that you call the central prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I did not call it. I was told by the men in uniform that that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not name it that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please point to your room, the room where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. My room was on the second floor. As you go upstairs, and as you walk up, it was to the left, on the left-hand side. I cannot pinpoint the window of that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was 12 to 15 metres long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my estimate. But the prisoners who were there said that it used to be some kind of a classroom. I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, if you cannot show it, you cannot.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I definitely cannot. I cannot be completely precise on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please tell me, the first time Mr. Naletilic came, who was with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time there were some men in uniform; some had white belts, some did not. They came. And as I said, they were at the door right inside the room, and they stayed only briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question to you: Who was in his company at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela, with him, and other soldiers and military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know, Your Honours. I apologise. I do not know if we shall be making a break now or not. I do not know your schedule, Your Honours. How did you plan this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: On this schedule, Mr. Krsnik, your time is up, unless Mr. Par will give some of his time to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we are making a break, then I shall talk with Mr. Krsnik, and we shall see how we shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just remember that in the order we issued about the scheduling, the Defence will have two hours together for the cross-examination. We'll resume at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I talked about it with my colleague. I won't take much longer, and then Mr. Par will continue, but we shall fit into the time set aside for us. And now I'd like to go back to that letter. I believe we all have it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have this letter which you wrote to the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Avdo Habib? If you do, I'd like to ask you -- one, two, three, four, fifth passage in your letter -- no. Sorry, fourth, fourth paragraph. See it? And it begins like this -- I'll try to read slowly: "I left on the 31st of March, 1993. I carry out my tasks in Germany, most of them, and as agreed, I have written to Bosnia after two months." And then you go on: "On my way back to Travnik with complete documentation, I was arrested in Split on the 24th." Their Honours and my learned friends can see in their English translation that the month is illegible. And in the Croat text, it is legible enough to see that it is either the sixth or the eighth month. Everybody in this courtroom and Their Honours can see it, but it is definitely not the fifth month of 1993. It doesn't say "05." So my question to you is: When exactly were you arrested in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested in Split on the 1st of June, 1993. And in this letter, it must be the mistake, whoever wrote it, whoever typed it, because I cannot type either on a typewriter or on a computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you then turn to page 2 and tell us -- don't, of course, say it aloud, because we are in a public session, but is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you dictate this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did dictate it. But it is a misprint. You know how it happens. Typos can be found in Globus and Vecernji List and Oslobodenje, and so on and so forth, let alone in an ordinary letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was my last question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Par, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon or good evening, Witness UU.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Zelimir Par, and I'm one of the counsel for Vinko Martinovic. I will ask you some questions relating to your today's testimony. You said that you saw Vinko Martinovic at the Heliodrom on several occasions and that he was amongst the detainees. Vinko Martinovic says that he was never at the Heliodrom nor did he ever visit any detainees, and we have not heard it either from other witnesses. So my question to you is -- and it is related to the specific incident that you described when a detainee from Prozor was beaten: Can you tell us who else was with Vinko Martinovic on that occasion and whom you allegedly saw? Can you list once again the persons who were with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Juka Prazina; there was Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta; Vinko Martinovic, Stela; Armin Pohara; Rusmir Agacevic. But please, I do not know Mr. Vinko Martinovic, Stela. It was what the detainees talked amongst themselves. They said, "Oh, there's Stela." I did not know him personally. I did not know him before. So I could not conclude for myself that that was the gentleman's name. So it was the detainees who were talking amongst themselves and said that yes, it was he, that he was together with the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I understand that. But on all those occasions that you say you saw him, was it at the same level of your personal knowledge? I don't know if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is always the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are still talking about this incident where the man from Prozor was beaten. Do you know who was the first one to hit him, before Prazina and the dog and all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the soldiers in a multicoloured uniform. I am quite sure it was not Vinko Martinovic, Stela, who struck him, nor later. Nor later he did not beat him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. I'm asking you this because of this Aleksovski, you see. In your statement which you saw today, you described this event. And in addition to these names which you gave us, you also mentioned this Aleksovski. You also said that Aleksovski was the first one to strike the man from Prozor. Do I have to show you the statement once again, or can you confirm that it is true that that is what you said in your statement of the 17th and 18th of September, 1997? Is it true that you said that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is true that I said it, but I cannot remember every single detail after eight years. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, right. I understand that. But we are still dealing with this Aleksovski. And I'm asking you now, you omitted him today, and yet you mentioned him in your statement. So my question is: Did you find out later that this Zlatko Aleksovski was charged before this Tribunal for events in Central Bosnia where he was in -- until 1994 and that in 1993, he could not be where you say he was? Is it what you heard about him, and is that why you omitted him from your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear about that, nor do I have any idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the form of that question, Your Honour. It assumes facts not in evidence, and I think that we would not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be in a position to agree that Mr. Aleksovski could not have been down in the Mostar area during that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, why is it, then, that you do not mention Aleksovski today, yet your statement teems with this name, especially in relation to Vinko Martinovic? So my question is: Is there any particular reason for which Aleksovski was omitted from your today's testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there, therefore, any reason why he was mentioned then and is not mentioned now? You've got to explain it to me somehow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply I must explain that even then, when I mentioned him, I mentioned him on the basis of what the detainees had told me. Because you must realise that I was lying down on the ground like a sack full of stones. I never moved. So somebody next to me says, "There's Aleksovski." If somebody says, "There's Madonna," I would have believed him. Do you understand what I'm trying to say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you. But do you understand me when you say the same thing you told me about Vinko Martinovic, that it was somebody who pointed and said, "That is Vinko Martinovic," and that you don't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But today, you mentioned him, and in the way in which you mentioned him. So my question is: Why this change with regard to Aleksovski? Why didn't you provide a similar explanation for Aleksovski, but he simply vanishes into thin air?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My objection, Your Honour, is that this question has been asked already by counsel. It has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We also believe that this question has been asked and answered. You must skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the same incident, the beaten detainee from Prozor. But let me ask you something about Rusmir Agacevic. You said that he was also present on that occasion. And my question is: Is there a conflict between you and Rusmir Agacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We have never had a conflict or hatred or argument, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me if there is or if you know of a reason that somebody -- the reason for which somebody else misused your name in the newspaper and started an argument with Agacevic? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there must be a reason certainly, because during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all sorts of things have been happening and still are happening. You know it better than I do, sir. And it is quite possible that one of the services -- and as you know, and I'm sure you know more than I do, there are about five, six services, and of the secret ones there can be 15, 20 of them, and I don't know how many we don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So let us move on now to something else, and that is Stela's men. You said that they came there, took some prisoners away, and so on. Tell me, do you know personally any of those so-called Stela's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know any of them personally. I never -- I've never seen them before, and I cannot give you any names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me -- and do you know about that unit anything? What was its name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know what the unit was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you then know what kind of uniforms or insignia did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I do know - and again I repeat, please do understand my point - it is those detainees who were together with me. They kept saying that it was something like Convicts Battalion. That is what I heard. As for the uniforms, there were many colours, with HVO patches. Some others may have had some other patches. I don't know. But as I have said, I was seldom close enough to be able to read it on their uniforms and say they had this or that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I am asking you these questions. Take it easy. Don't get upset. My question to you is whether there is a difference between these soldiers from others. Can you tell these men from others? And I'll ask you the same thing about Juka's men. Did you know anyone from Juka's unit personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I never did, nor did I ever see anyone from Juka's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you perhaps mix up Juka's and Tuta's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my mind, they were all the same. I don't know who was under whom and what was he like or what was he.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is just one more incident we have to cover with a few questions, so will you please focus on the situation in the infirmary when you were beaten. My colleague showed you this part of the statement where Aleksovski is mentioned but not Stela. But I'm not going to ask you about the statement. I'm going to ask you questions in relation to what you testified today. You said - and you will correct me if I'm wrong - you said that you saw Stela sitting in that infirmary whilst you were beaten by two soldiers with white belts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those soldiers with white belts, were they part of the military police? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody who had white belts was part of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And tell us, did Stela have a white belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not have a white belt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that those soldiers who beat you were not his men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I cannot really say that they were his men or Marko Markovic's or Juka's or Zuka's soldiers or who they were. I'm not -- I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not have any further questions. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, please, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just ask Mr. Par a question? You asked about Mr. Rusmir Agacevic. You asked him did he know him and was there any bad feeling between them. Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall explain it briefly. Rusmir Agacevic appears in this in relation to the article, and before that he is mentioned in the statement that the witness made. The witness said in the statement that Rusmir Agacevic used to come to the Heliodrom, a man who is a Muslim and who at that time allegedly had some role to play in relation to Muslims there. That is one thing. And in the article that was the subject of all sorts of misunderstandings today -- apart from that, he is an actor in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so a public figure. I do not know if that answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Is this gentleman mentioned in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he is mentioned in the statement as a man who was present when this detainee from Prozor was beaten. It is in the witness's statement of the 17th and 18th of September, 1997, and today the witness confirmed to me that this Rusmir Agacevic was present when this detainee from Prozor was beaten and that allegedly Vinko Martinovic was present on that occasion too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness UU, in relation to the letter which was shown to us a few minutes ago and which - thank you, Judge - which you were asked about, you talked about going from the centre of Bosnia to Germany for humanitarian assistance. Was this an official task that you were on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was more a private task, but it was also official because that was how I could get out, that is, get my travel documents, only if I said that from neighbours or friends, or I don't know who else, that I would go to them and ask them to send perhaps some food or clothing to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you tell the officials in Split and thereafter that you had actually been collecting humanitarian aid for the victims of the war in Central Bosnia, or did they know in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not know it and didn't ask me, and I didn't tell them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Stringer asked you if you had any idea of why you were arrested, detained, and treated so appallingly, and you said you didn't know but you formulated a possible reason, and that was that you came from Central Bosnia, which was the scene of a great deal of brutal behaviour on all sides, I believe. Were the other people who were with you treated in the same way, or were you selected to be the worst treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They treated brutally other men who were arrested. They beat them and insulted them. It just so happened that I suffered most, so that I was unable to move; again, perhaps, I say, because I come from Central Bosnia and because at that time, there was fighting going on in Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf. I mean fighting between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In relation to the treatment which was, according to your testimony, meted out to the young man from Prozor, was that the same sort of treatment that you received, abuse because you came from the scene of fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I cannot really say for sure. That could also be it. But I still think that somebody had recognised him, that is, that one of those soldiers in the HVO uniforms had recognised him, perhaps known him before, or perhaps on the spur of the moment, some incident or something had been fabri -- invented or provoked. I cannot really say why this battery, why this incident took place, but it is quite possible that it was as you put it. But again, it is also possible that that soldier knew this young man from before and wanted to take it out on him, or perhaps they staged some incident or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm always interested, Witness UU, in the application of the Geneva Convention in prisoner of war camps, and I always ask questions in relation to that. Can you tell me again what happened on the day that the International Red Cross representatives came to the hospital -- or to the Heliodrom? To the best of your recollection, can you go through that again for me, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I claim responsibly that two or three persons, when they came to the Heliodrom -- and please understand me. Maybe they had been to the Heliodrom a hundred times. But to the room in which I spent 45 days there, I saw them only twice. Of those two times, what happened in so-called hangars or some other buildings or rooms, I know nothing about that, and I cannot say anything about that. But when they came to the door - and I say this responsibly - and when they started talking - the detainees, I mean, they started saying, "Here's the Red Cross" - they all jumped up these like starving children of Biafra. They all rushed towards them, and I stayed just behind there lying down as a bag, as a chair, as a table, as a rock. Now, can you imagine, it's 50 or 60 detainees surrounding the three of them. You could not see them at all. But I am quite positive that at that time, many soldiers with white belts entered. And after 20 minutes or so, they drove the Red Cross out of that room. Where the Red Cross went then, I do not know. Perhaps to other rooms. Perhaps they didn't; perhaps they did. But what I can say under full responsibility is that this is 100 percent truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness UU, when the Red Cross came, was there no arrangement made that there would be a desk on which papers could be placed and one of the representatives could sit at a chair and take your names in an orderly manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 100 percent in the room where I was, no table or chairs were organised or anything like that. Now, whether that happened in other rooms in other buildings, in the so-called hangars, as they used to call them, that I do not know. Perhaps yes; perhaps no. I have no problem with that. But I say 100 percent that did not happen in my room, and that normal access of the representatives of the Red Cross was not possible. I never moved to any other rooms. I do not know what happened in the Heliodrom compound except for what I was told occasionally by some other prisoners. If that's what they said it was, I just accepted it at face value, and that's what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Am I correct in recalling that you said to Mr. Krsnik that documents were torn up by the men in white belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Some prisoners came and said, "What is the use of my being registered by the Red Cross when they tore up this card, this ID card, the card I had?" And the others would say, "It doesn't matter. You are still registered in a computer." This is the extent of the conversations that I was able to hear, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'll move on to something totally different, a subject that caused a lot of problem today. I wonder if not the article but the magazine could be placed on the ELMO so that you could see it, and I want you to tell me, do you recognise this magazine? Have you ever seen it or read it? Do you know anything at all about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do not want to comment on this magazine because I never saw it. I never held it in my hand. And I take full responsibility when I say that this is not my doing, that I have nothing to do with it. And I do not want to make any comment about that magazine because, as I said 1.000 times, it happens every day in the press that Miroslav Ciro Blazevic, a well-known coach, he says, "I do not want to deal with the journalists, with the press any more because they impute all kinds of things." And you know what happens in times of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness UU, I'm not asking you about the article. I'm asking you about the magazine. And I want you to look at the cover of that magazine and want you to say whether you have ever seen that magazine before. I'm not asking you about the article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you please show me the cover of the magazine so that I can look at it, and I will give you my reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just the cover, sir. That's all I want you to look at. We're not talking about the article. I just want you to tell me, have you ever seen the magazine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please show me the cover, and I will give you the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could we see the date, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the cover page very well, and I take full responsibility in saying that I have never read this magazine. I never held it in my hand, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not this issue nor any other issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It looks like an satirical magazine, from the cover. That's all I wanted you to say, just had you ever seen this particular magazine or the publication before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We can take it off the ELMO now. One last thing, Witness. This is for my own curiosity. How are you now? Have your injuries recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will say as an honourable person that I have still serious consequences. I cannot sleep more than two or three hours in a 24-hour cycle. I have days and nights when I cannot get up. I feel pain in my legs, in my arms. I do receive some medical help, some medications, some injection. I have to say that I do receive those. But my mental condition, my health condition is close to zero. I feel pain at any change. I mostly suffer from insomnia, and I cannot shake off the question of why I had to suffer when I never belonged to any kind of organisation. I was part of no military. I was not involved in anything. My father only gave me this name 40-odd years ago, and this is why I have suffered, and this is why my family, my mother, my brothers, my sisters, my father are still suffering. And I have these pains day and night, but I am not giving up. I believe that it will improve. The wounds have healed to a large degree, but I'm still not well. I cannot walk for more than ten minutes at a time, and it's hard. But I thank you for asking me this question and thank you for showing understanding for my unfortunate case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I can appreciate, Witness, that the psychological trauma is continuing, and indeed the sequelae of your other injuries. In all the circumstances, therefore, thank you very much for answering my questions and indeed for coming here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. Judge Diarra?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I would simply like to ask you: Did you have any opportunity to check, to verify whether the persons of whom you were told that they were Messrs. Naletilic and Martinovic were indeed these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no opportunity to verify whether Mr. Martinovic, called Stela, and Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, were indeed these men. I had no opportunity to verify it. I did not verify it. And again I take full responsibility when I say that even before that, I had never seen them, and I never had any conflict or any problems with them. And I believe that they had none with me either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at this point in time, you know that Mr. -- that Vinko Martinovic and Mladen Naletilic passed through the prison, the camp where you were staying because you were told so by the other prisoners who were there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is exactly right, because all my knowledge is based on what they told me. And they were talking among themselves quietly, whispering. They were sharing stories, the prisoners who were from Herzegovina, Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, Bijelo Polje, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Juka Prazina turned loose his German shepherd dog on this prisoner from Prozor, this happened in the presence of Martinovic, that is, you said that you thought that this man was Martinovic. Was Naletilic also present there, and how did these people react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was present. But please, I did not hear what they were talking about, and I did not see what their reaction was. After a period of time, they pushed him out of the room into the hallway, and I will take responsibility in saying that the other prisoners who were there, and I -- they saw that Vinko Martinovic, Stela, and Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, did not beat or abuse this young man. But I do not know how they reacted. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were not near me. They may have been 12 to 15 metres away from me. I do not know what they were talking about and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you the only member of your family who survived these difficult times which took place in your country, or did other members of your family, your brothers, sisters, or parents, also suffered some hard times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm the only one who had suffered in this way, in a camp. My brothers, my father, my sisters were not in a camp. But, for instance, perhaps some distant relatives or some neighbours of mine may have suffered in another way, may have been wounded by some shrapnel or something, or in conflict with the Serbian army and so on. But of my family, I was the only one who was imprisoned and mistreated and tortured and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point, you told us about your only child. In a letter which you wrote to the Minister, you mentioned two children. So do you have one or two children, and were these children also children also the victims of the traumas that you suffered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have two children. My children are victims, and my wife, for days and nights -- day and night, they empathise with what I have gone through. They often ask me questions. I often avoid giving them the real truth. Frequently, a small detail may make me raise my voice, or I may turn depressive or aggressive, and the children start crying and run to their mother. I am not trying to beat my children or mistreat them in any way, but these things are happening. It's this so-called post-traumatic stress syndrome. So they are victims because they empathise with me. When I am unwell, when the doctors come to give me injection, when I take medication, when I cannot get up, when at night there's no physician, when I have to wait for the morning in order to be able to get some injection, then they cannot sleep. They cannot have a normal, regular life like children should have. And you will know fully well that they are at no fault in all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, sir, and I wish you a lot of courage and a lot of good fortune to you and your children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Diarra. Any questions out of Judge's questions? Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, just one question of the witness. Further examination by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you again, you were asked about how you knew that it was Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and Vinko Martinovic, Stela. And I just wanted to ask you: The two men whom you're saying are Naletilic and Martinovic, did you see those two men in your part of the building with your own eyes and then learn from others who you think the names of those men are? Did you see them with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct, that I saw them with my own eyes. But I did not know who they were. Then the prisoners told me, "These are Vinko Martinovic, Juka Prazina. That is Mr. Mladen Naletilic," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions? Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, thank you very much for helping us by giving your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, are there any documents to tender into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just Exhibit 20.10 as marked, which is /3, 20.10/3. I think that the Exhibit Number 1 I think is already in evidence and the Trial Chamber is able to find all the locations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But it was re-marked by the witness himself. That should be a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That would be P1/1, and we tender that exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess there's no objections from Defence counsel. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, Your Honours, the Defence would like to tender the letter, but I do not have enough copies, so I will provide a sufficient number of copies and give it to the Madam Registrar tomorrow. I would just like to announce that I will tender it. That would be D1/40, I believe, Madam Registrar, the letter to the Minister. Then D1/39. And I am going to provide the sufficient number of copies to the Madam Registrar tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. No objection to the Defence exhibit. Before we break, I would just like to express on behalf of the Prosecution our gratitude to the Trial Chamber and your staff for your willingness to work late and to do this. We really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. How about that previous statement put forward by you during the cross-examination? We believe that you used that document quite extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I will not take it badly. I know that I have -- that I'm running out of yellow cards, but I did not have enough copies. So when we produce enough copies, I'm going to tender that previous statement, too, as our exhibit. And that would, I believe, be D1/40 is our next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I just simply want to say, Mr. President, if we're talking about the OTP statement which is dated the 17th and 18th of September, 1997, we have no objection to it being tendered, I think, for the limited purposes which would fall within an earlier decision of this Trial Chamber, although the Trial Chamber can obviously accept it for whatever evidentiary value it deems worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you could submit this document to this Trial Chamber, and Madam Registrar will give it an ID number. Whether this should be admitted into evidence, we'll make the decision at a later stage, after we read those previous statements. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very clear, Your Honours. I was just going to ask you one more thing: Is your decision a standing decision that only the relevant parts of the statement be taken into account? This is back a couple of months ago, this decision. Because I know that my learned friend only was leading the relevant portions, I believe, if I'm not wrong. My learned friend will remember that -- that the decision, the ruling of the Trial Chamber was only that the relevant portions of the statements be retained, be kept. If that is not so, I'll be happy to provide the full -- to finish a full statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you used very extensively this previous statement, and you can submit that statement in its totality. We will make the decision at a later stage concerning this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we will resume at 2.30 tomorrow afternoon in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
